estrogen.title: Estrogen
estrogen.glance: Estrogen is a key hormone that helps prepare your body for a possible pregnancy each cycle.
estrogen.overview:
Estrogen is one of the main hormones behind the menstrual cycle. In the first half of the cycle
(the follicular phase) its level rises as a follicle in the ovary matures. This rise thickens the
lining of the uterus and leads up to ovulation.

Estrogen also influences things you might notice day to day — energy, mood, and changes in
cervical mucus around your fertile days. After ovulation its level dips and then shifts again,
working alongside another hormone, progesterone, through the second half of the cycle.

Levels naturally rise and fall across each cycle, and they change across life stages too. This is
normal — it's the rhythm your body runs on, not something to "fix."
estrogen.deep:
Estrogen isn't a single substance but a group of related hormones (the most active in the cycle
is estradiol). Most of it is made by the ovaries, in the growing follicle. Its cyclical rise and
fall — together with progesterone, and the brain's signalling hormones LH and FSH — is what
drives the phases of the cycle. Because estrogen touches many systems, its natural shifts can
show up in small ways throughout the month; tracking helps you learn your own pattern rather than
compare it to an "average."

follicular-phase.title: Follicular phase
follicular-phase.glance: The follicular phase is the first half of the cycle, when an egg ripens and the womb lining thickens.
follicular-phase.overview:
The follicular phase is the first part of the cycle. It begins on the first day of your period and
runs up to ovulation. Its name comes from the follicle — the small fluid-filled sac in the ovary
that holds and grows an egg during this time.

Through this phase the hormone estrogen rises. That rising estrogen does two main things: it helps
a follicle in the ovary mature, and it thickens the lining of the uterus (womb), getting the body
ready in case a pregnancy begins later in the cycle.

Because estrogen is climbing, some people notice more energy or changes in cervical mucus as the
fertile days approach. Everyone's experience is different, and none of it needs "managing" — it's
simply the first half of your cycle doing its work.
follicular-phase.deep:
The follicular phase can vary in length from cycle to cycle, which is part of why whole cycles
differ from person to person and month to month. It ends when rising estrogen helps trigger the
release of an egg (ovulation). Because its final days lead into ovulation, this is when the fertile
window opens — which is why the end of the follicular phase matters for anyone tracking fertility.

luteal-phase.title: Luteal phase
luteal-phase.glance: The luteal phase is the second half of the cycle, after ovulation, when progesterone rises.
luteal-phase.overview:
The luteal phase is the part of the cycle that follows ovulation and runs until your next period
begins. It's named after the corpus luteum — the small structure the ovary forms from the empty
follicle once the egg has been released.

In this phase the hormone progesterone rises. Its job is to keep the lining of the uterus (womb)
thick and settled, so that if a fertilised egg arrives it has somewhere to implant. Estrogen stays
part of the picture too, working alongside progesterone.

If no pregnancy begins, the corpus luteum breaks down, progesterone and estrogen fall, and the
lining is no longer maintained — which brings on your next period and starts a new cycle. This is
also the stretch when some people notice premenstrual changes in mood, sleep or the body.
luteal-phase.deep:
The luteal phase tends to be a little steadier in length than the first half of the cycle, often
running somewhere in the region of about two weeks, though there's normal variation from person to
person. Because its end is tied to the fall in progesterone, the arrival of a period is really the
visible sign that hormone levels have dropped. Tracking how you feel across the luteal phase can
help you tell apart what's a familiar pattern for you from what's new or worth a conversation with
a clinician.

menstrual-cycle.title: The menstrual cycle
menstrual-cycle.glance: The menstrual cycle is the monthly rhythm your body runs on to prepare for a possible pregnancy.
menstrual-cycle.overview:
The menstrual cycle is counted from the first day of your period — that's day 1 — up to the day
before your next period starts. It's driven by hormones that rise and fall in a repeating pattern
each month.

A cycle is often around 28 days, but that's just an average. Anywhere from about 21 to 35 days is
normal, and your own length can vary a little from month to month. Learning your own pattern is
more useful than comparing it to a number.

Across the cycle your body moves through a few stages: your period, the build-up to releasing an
egg, the release itself (ovulation), and the stretch afterwards. Each stage is shaped by
hormones, mainly estrogen and progesterone.
menstrual-cycle.deep:
The whole cycle is a conversation between the brain and the ovaries, carried by hormones. In the
first half, estrogen rises as an egg-containing follicle matures in the ovary and the lining of
the uterus (womb) thickens. Around the middle of the cycle an egg is released. In the second half,
progesterone helps keep that lining ready in case a fertilised egg arrives.

If there's no pregnancy, estrogen and progesterone fall to low levels, the lining is shed as your
period, and the pattern begins again. Because these hormones touch many systems, you may notice
small day-to-day changes across the month — this is the normal rhythm of the cycle, not something
to "fix."

menstrual-phase.title: Menstrual phase (your period)
menstrual-phase.glance: Your period is the few days of bleeding that begin each cycle, as the womb lining is shed.
menstrual-phase.overview:
The menstrual phase is your period — the days when you bleed. It starts on day 1 of the cycle,
when the levels of estrogen and progesterone have dropped low enough that the lining built up
inside the uterus (womb) is no longer maintained and comes away, leaving the body through the
vagina.

A period usually lasts about 2 to 7 days, with roughly 5 days being typical. Flow is often
heaviest in the first couple of days and lighter after that. Periods commonly begin around age 12,
though starting earlier or later is also normal.

What's "normal" varies a lot from person to person. Tracking your own periods helps you notice
what's usual for you, which is far more meaningful than any average.
menstrual-phase.deep:
The bleeding of a period is the lining of the uterus (the endometrium) being shed after a cycle
where no pregnancy has begun. It marks both the end of one cycle and the start of the next, which
is why day 1 of your period is counted as day 1 of the whole cycle. As your period finishes,
estrogen begins to rise again and the body starts rebuilding the lining for the cycle ahead.

ovulation.title: Ovulation
ovulation.glance: Ovulation is when an ovary releases an egg — the most fertile point of your cycle.
ovulation.overview:
Ovulation is the moment an ovary releases a mature egg. It's the turning point of the cycle: the
first half builds up to it, and the second half follows it.

In a cycle of about 28 days, ovulation often happens around day 14 — but the timing varies. A
helpful way to think about it is that ovulation usually occurs somewhere from 10 to 16 days before
your next period starts. It can be hard to pinpoint the exact day.

Once released, an egg can be fertilised for only about 12 to 24 hours. Sperm, though, can survive
in the body for several days, so the "fertile window" is wider than a single day — roughly the few
days leading up to ovulation and the day itself.
ovulation.deep:
The release of the egg is triggered by a short, sharp rise in hormones around mid-cycle, following
the estrogen build-up of the follicular phase. Because sperm can live for a number of days while
the egg lives less than a day, pregnancy is most likely from sex in the days just before
ovulation. Ovulation can shift from cycle to cycle with things like stress or illness, which is
why predicting it exactly is difficult and why tracking several cycles is more reliable than any
single calculation.

progesterone.title: Progesterone
progesterone.glance: Progesterone is the hormone of the cycle's second half, preparing the womb lining after ovulation.
progesterone.overview:
Progesterone is one of the main hormones behind the menstrual cycle, and it takes the lead in the
second half — after an egg is released at ovulation.

Its main role is to help the lining of the uterus (womb) stay thick and ready, so that if a
fertilised egg arrives it can implant and a pregnancy can begin. In this way progesterone works as
a partner to estrogen, which did much of the build-up earlier in the cycle.

If no pregnancy begins, progesterone levels fall. That drop is what allows the lining to be shed
as your next period. The rise and fall of progesterone across the second half of the cycle is a
normal, expected rhythm.
progesterone.deep:
Progesterone is produced mainly by the corpus luteum — the structure the ovary forms from the
follicle after it has released its egg. This is why progesterone rises specifically in the luteal
(post-ovulation) phase. When the corpus luteum breaks down, progesterone and estrogen both fall,
signalling the start of a new cycle. Its natural shifts are part of why some people notice
premenstrual changes in the days before a period.
